sections.description: This section covers the initial patient encounter, the recognition of systemic inflammatory markers, and the identification of key 'clues' that suggest both systemic and metabolic disturbances.
subtopics: Analysis of presenting symptoms: Fever, headache, arthralgia, and malaise
Recognizing mucocutaneous hallmarks: Oral aphthae and folliculitis-like rashes
Interpreting 'hidden' signs of hyponatremia: Persistent hiccups and rhabdomyolysis (elevated CK)
Initial laboratory findings: Markers of inflammation (CRP, ESR) and metabolic derangements (Hyperglycemia, Hyponatremia)

sections.description: This section focuses on the systemic diagnosis of BD, explaining the clinical criteria and the significance of the mucocutaneous findings presented in the case.
subtopics: Pathophysiology of Behçet's Disease: A multisystem inflammatory disorder
Applying the International Criteria for Behçet's Disease (ICBD) scoring system
Clinical significance of genital aphthosis as a highly specific marker
The role and limitations of HLA-B51 testing in the diagnosis of BD

sections.description: This section explores the neurological manifestations of BD, focusing on how to diagnose neuro-BD even in the absence of characteristic imaging findings.
subtopics: Clinical phenotypes of Neuro-BD: Parenchymal lesions vs. aseptic meningitis
Interpreting Brain MRI in early neuro-BD: Why a normal MRI does not exclude the diagnosis
Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) analysis: Identifying lymphocytic pleocytosis and increased protein
Temporal patterns of Neuro-BD: Comparing concurrent onset vs. delayed onset relative to systemic BD

sections.description: This section explains the pathophysiology of the Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone secretion (SIADH) and its specific association with central nervous system inflammation in this case.
subtopics: Laboratory diagnosis of SIADH: Serum and urine osmolality, urinary sodium, and ADH levels
The pathophysiology of euvolemic hyponatremia
The role of pro-inflammatory cytokines (specifically IL-6) in triggering ADH release during CNS inflammation
Distinguishing neuro-inflammatory SIADH from drug-induced SIADH in BD patients

sections.description: This section details the process of elimination used by clinicians to rule out other causes of fever, meningitis, and hyponatremia.
subtopics: Excluding CNS infections: Viral (HSV, VZV), bacterial, and tuberculous meningitis
Evaluating neoplastic causes: Rule-out of primary CNS malignancy and CNS lymphoma using MRI and CSF cytology
Screening for other autoimmune/inflammatory mimics: Sarcoidosis (ACE levels) and other connective tissue diseases
Interpreting non-specific markers: The clinical utility and limitations of soluble interleukin-2 receptor (sIL-2R)

sections.description: This section discusses the treatment strategy employed for this patient, the pharmacological role of colchicine, and the management of acute hyponatremia.
subtopics: Conservative management of SIADH: Fluid restriction and the risks of rapid sodium correction
Colchicine monotherapy: Mechanism of action (inhibiting neutrophil migration and IL-6 production)
Comparing colchicine with corticosteroids and immunosuppressants in the treatment of Neuro-BD
Long-term follow-up and the integration of comorbid management (e.g., Type 2 Diabetes)
